title: 6 Powerful Ways To Build Community
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Building on a previous article's three conditions for genuine classroom community — an enticing goal, universal need for every member, and a real chance of failure — Linsin offers six concrete ways to put those conditions into practice. The ideas include finding a rival classroom for friendly competition, performing at school events, competing in schoolwide contests, pursuing a fixed academic achievement goal as a class, serving the school community through projects like gardens or murals, and simply having fun together through lighthearted, shared activities. He stresses that a teacher's own enthusiasm is the key ingredient that makes any of these goals feel enticing enough for students to rally around. The article closes by clarifying that competition itself is not the point; the value comes from students working together toward a shared goal that creates camaraderie and belonging.
points: Genuine classroom community grows from students voluntarily working together toward a shared goal, not from being told to be nice.
Practical community-builders include classroom rivalries, public performances, schoolwide competitions, class-wide academic goals, and service projects.
A teacher's visible enthusiasm for a shared goal is the ingredient that makes students actually invest in it.
It is the process of working together toward a goal — not winning or losing — that produces camaraderie and belonging.
quotes: Having a classroom to compete against offers ready-made goals and countless opportunities to build community.
Create a fixed academic goal for your class to pursue. It can be the number of books read, perfect scores on spelling quizzes, percentage improvement on math tests, or whatever you choose.
Beautify the school by growing a garden, painting a mural, or cleaning up campus. Your students will feel good about helping their school, and you’ll have a rewarding goal for them to rally around.

It’s important to sell each of the goals you decide on and make them enticing enough to your students that they’ll shake like wet Chihuahuas. They must be excited and want to achieve the goals you set for them.
It isn’t winning or losing that builds community. It is working together toward an exciting goal that creates camaraderie, encourages teamwork, and causes a strong sense of belonging.
